value.overview: The Three-wattled Bellbird is a striking Central American songbird named for the three long, fleshy wattles hanging from the adult male’s bill. Males are mainly chestnut and olive-green, with a pale head, while females are smaller, greener, and lack wattles. Its extremely loud, ringing call can carry over long distances. The species depends largely on mature mountain forests and is an important long-distance disperser of large forest fruits.
value.classification: The Three-wattled Bellbird belongs to the family Cotingidae, which includes many fruit-eating tropical forest birds. Its scientific name is Procnias tricarunculatus.
value.identification: Adult males have three prominent blackish or dark brown wattles at the base of the bill, a pale to whitish head, chestnut-brown underparts, and olive-green wings and back. Females are duller green overall and lack the wattles. The species is usually detected by its extraordinarily loud, clear, metallic call rather than by sight. Its heavy bill and upright posture are also characteristic. Immature birds resemble females and gradually develop adult male plumage and wattles.
value.rangeHabitat: The Three-wattled Bellbird is restricted to the highlands of southern Central America, occurring from Nicaragua through Costa Rica and Panama into western Colombia. In Costa Rica it is principally associated with montane and premontane forests, forest edges, and areas containing fruiting trees, especially along the Cordillera de Tilarán, Cordillera Volcánica Central, and Cordillera de Talamanca. It uses higher-elevation forests during the breeding season and may move to lower foothills, Caribbean slopes, and other forested lowlands at other times of year.
value.migrationStatus: It is an altitudinal migrant. In Costa Rica, many birds move seasonally between high-elevation breeding areas and lower-elevation forests, with movements varying among regions and individuals rather than following one single route.
value.breeding: Breeding occurs mainly during the wet season, when fruit resources are abundant. Males gather in traditional display areas or leks and advertise with their powerful bell-like calls; they may also perform conspicuous movements while displaying their wattles. Females select mates and are responsible for nest construction, incubation, and most care of the young. The nest is a small platform placed in a tree, and breeding success depends on suitable forest structure and abundant fruiting vegetation.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of fruits, especially large fruits produced by native forest trees. The species can swallow relatively large fruits and transport seeds considerable distances, making it an important seed disperser in mountain forests. It occasionally takes insects and other small animal food, particularly when feeding young. Birds often forage quietly in the canopy and may travel between separated fruiting trees or forest patches.
value.behavior: Three-wattled Bellbirds are generally solitary outside breeding displays, although several birds may gather where fruit is plentiful. Males are especially conspicuous during the breeding season because of their far-carrying calls and display behavior. The species spends much of its time in the canopy, where its green plumage can provide camouflage. Seasonal movements allow it to track fruit supplies and connect different elevations within the landscape.

conservation.populationTrend: The population is considered to be declining.
conservation.threats: Major concerns include loss, fragmentation, and degradation of montane and premontane forest; removal of large fruiting trees; and the disruption of seasonal movement routes between breeding and nonbreeding areas. Climate change may further alter fruiting patterns, suitable elevations, and the availability of connected forest. Habitat loss in both breeding and nonbreeding areas is particularly important because the species depends on several parts of the landscape during its annual cycle.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore mature mountain forest and maintain connected habitat between highlands and lower-elevation forests. Retain native fruiting trees, especially large canopy trees, and support protected areas and habitat corridors in Costa Rica and throughout the species’ range. Bird monitoring, protection of known breeding and display sites, responsible ecotourism, and planting native species can also help. Avoid disturbing displaying males and encourage land management that preserves seasonal movement routes.
